title: BOOK FOUR / CHAPTER ONE. On the principles of human salvation, namely the grace of paternal mercy
latin: LIBER QUARTUS, De principiis & mediis humanae salutis. CAPUT PRIMUM, De principiis humanae salutis, & quidem nominatim de gratia paternae miserationis. HActenus tribus libris persecuti sumus tum naturam & constitutionem S. Theologiae, tum ultimum absoluteque summum hominis finem, supernaturalem videlicet animae & corporis illius beatitudinem, tum denique 1. hominis creationem, qua Deus eum huic summo fini consequendo fecerat idoneum, iustitia nempe & innocentia praeditum, ut, posteaquam in sincero constantique amore & cultu creatoris vitam citra aerumnas iucundam & quietam egisset, immortalis sine sensu mortis in caelestem aeternamque & absolute beatam transmitteretur; 2. defectionem eius, quando videlicet suasu & impulsu Satanae suaque simul imprudentia amiserit beatitudinem, ad quam divinitus erat ordinatus, & creatorem suum inobedientia nefaria offenderit, ut iam non aeternae vitae, sed aeternae mortis heres factus fuerit, & tanquam reus laesae maiestatis divinae, omnibus iis donis, quae supra naturae suae conditionem acceperat, non possit per se viam illam videre, invenire ac tenere, qua ad beatitudinem ipsi in principio destinatam ferat. I. Sequuntur iam principia, a quibus salus aeterna dependet, & nihil aliud sunt, quam actus divinae gratiae, qua Dei misericordia & iustitia ita temperantur, ut homo peccator iram Dei & damnationem effugere, & amicitiam Dei vitamque aeternam postliminio consequi possit.
english: BOOK FOUR. On the principles and means of human salvation.
CHAPTER ONE. On the principles of human salvation, and namely on the grace of paternal mercy.

Thus far in three books we have treated the nature and constitution of sacred theology; then the last and absolutely highest end of the human being — namely the supernatural blessedness of soul and body; and finally (1) the humans creation, by which God made him fit to attain this highest end, endowed with righteousness and innocence, so that after living a pleasant and quiet life in sincere and constant love and worship of the Creator without hardships he might be transferred, immortal and without sense of death, into heavenly, eternal, and absolutely blessed life; and (2) his defection, when by Satans persuasion and impulse and by his own imprudence he lost the blessedness to which he had been divinely ordered, and offended his Creator by wicked disobedience, so that he became heir not of eternal life but of eternal death, and as one guilty of divine majesty lese-majeste, stripped of those gifts received above his natures condition, cannot by himself see, find, and keep that way which leads to the blessedness destined for him at the beginning.

I. There follow now the principles on which eternal salvation depends; and they are nothing other than acts of divine grace, by which Gods mercy and justice are so tempered that the sinful human can escape Gods wrath and damnation and regain Gods friendship and eternal life.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): and they stand as nothing other than acts belonging toward divine grace, by which Gods mercy and justice stand as so tempered that ye sinful human can escape Gods wrath and damnation and regain Gods friendship and eternal life. — There follow now ye principles on which eternal salvation depends; — I. — and (2) his defection, when by Satans persuasion and impulse and by his own imprudence he lost ye blessedness to which he had been divinely ordered, and offended his Creator by wicked disobedience, so that he became heir not belonging toward eternal life but belonging toward eternal death, and as one guilty belonging toward divine majesty lese-majeste, stripped belonging toward those gifts received above his natures condition, cannot by himself see, find, and keep that way which leads to ye blessedness destined toward him at ye beginning. — and finally (1) ye humans creation, by which God made him fit to attain this highest end, endowed with righteousness and innocence, so that after living a pleasant and quiet life in sincere and constant love and worship belonging toward ye Creator without hardships he might be transferred, immortal and without sense belonging toward death, into heavenly, eternal, and absolutely blessed life; — then ye last and absolutely highest end belonging toward ye human being — namely ye supernatural blessedness belonging toward soul and body; — Thus far in three books we have treated ye nature and constitution belonging toward sacred theology; — On ye principles belonging toward human salvation, and namely on ye grace belonging toward paternal mercy. — CHAPTER ONE. — On ye principles and means belonging toward human salvation. — BOOK FOUR.

title: II. Three principles of salvation; grace as free favor, not infused habit
latin: II. Sunt autem principia salutis humanae gratia tum paternae miserationis, tum fraternae redemtionis, tum supernae Dei vocationis. Cum salus nostra & Dei amicitia prorsus sit desperata sive nos convertamus ad nos ipsos, sive ad alias creaturas cunctas aut singulas, propterea quod iustitia Dei, cuius praeceptum violavimus, sic nullo modo possit fieri satis: primum profecto huius amicitiae salutisque nostrae principium est gratia Dei, qua non significamus generalem illam Dei beneficentiam, per quam res omnes creatae conservantur & gubernantur. Haec enim sibi nihilominus constaret, etiamsi homo in gratiam receptus nunquam fuisset. Intelligimus vero per eam actus divinae benevolentiae & philanthropiae, qua Deus humani generis lapsi misertus est, quando vidit id totum aeterno exitio immergi, neque ullo pacto ex eo liberari posse, nisi ipse succurreret, Eph. 1:5; 2:4; Tit. 3:4. Unde primo manifestum est, cum divinae literae dicunt, gratia nos salvos factos esse, per gratiam non intelligendam esse nisi misericordiam Dei & gratuitum erga nos favorem. Ideoque & repudiandam esse Pontificiorum acceptionem, qui gratiam hic interpretantur infusam qualitatem aut habitum quendam, sive is sit habitus charitatis, aut alius a charitate distinctus. Haec autem gratia ipsa data nobis fuit in Christo ante tempora secularia, 2 Tim. 1:9. Neque in dubium vocandum est, quin Deus lapsum hominis, etiamsi in tempore contigerit, tamen ante omnia tempora praesciverit, adeoque miserias & poenas, quibus genus humanum implicandum erat, praeviderit; secundò, quin etiam quemadmodum Deus hominum in tempore misertus est, ita quoque eo ipso, quo miserias praevidit, ab aeterno misertus fuerit, & quando subvenire vellet, decreverit. Verum enimvero, cum Deus non solum bonus sit, verum etiam iustus & constans in dictis suis, non potest fieri, quin pro peccatis poenam exigat severissimam, certissimeque impleri debeat quod ipse pronunciaverat: quocunque die comederis fructum vetitum, morte morieris. Quapropter necessarium est quam maxime, ut statuamus, a Deo secundum suam quidem misericordiam sic decretum de hominibus liberandis factum esse, ne tamen veritas & iustitia eius ullo modo violaretur. Ex quo colligimus, salutis nostrae principium revera esse admirandam humanaeque rationi impervestigabilem misericordiae & iustitiae divinae temperationem, ut videlicet huic ita satis fiat, quo tamen illi quoque suus sit locus ad succurrendum miseris.
english: II. The principles of human salvation are the grace of paternal mercy, of fraternal redemption, and of Gods heavenly calling.

Since our salvation and Gods friendship are wholly desperate whether we turn to ourselves or to all or any other creatures — because Gods justice, whose precept we violated, cannot otherwise be satisfied — the first principle of this friendship and of our salvation is truly Gods grace. By this we do not mean that general beneficence of God by which all created things are conserved and governed; for that would stand even if the human had never been received into grace. We mean rather the acts of divine benevolence and philanthropy by which God pitied the fallen human race when He saw it wholly sunk in eternal ruin and unable to be freed from it unless He Himself came to its aid (Ephesians 1:5; 2:4; Titus 3:4).

First, therefore, when the divine writings say we have been saved by grace, by grace is to be understood nothing but Gods mercy and free favor toward us. And so the Papists sense must be rejected, who here interpret grace as an infused quality or habit — whether the habit of charity or another distinct from charity. This grace itself was given us in Christ before the ages of the world (2 Timothy 1:9). Nor is it to be doubted that God foresaw the humans fall before all times, even though it happened in time, and so foresaw the miseries and punishments in which the human race was to be entangled; and second, that just as God pitied humans in time, so by the very foresight of those miseries He pitied from eternity and decreed when He would help.

Yet since God is not only good but also just and constant in His words, it cannot be that He fail to exact the severest punishment for sins, and what He Himself pronounced must most certainly be fulfilled: in whatever day you eat the forbidden fruit, you shall die the death. Therefore it is most necessary to hold that Gods decree to free humans was made according to His mercy in such a way that His truth and justice were in no way violated. From this we gather that the principle of our salvation is truly an admirable tempering of divine mercy and justice, unsearchable to human reason — so that justice is satisfied, and yet mercy also has its place to help the wretched.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Nor stands as it to be doubted that God foresaw ye humans fall before all times, even though it happened in time, and so foresaw ye miseries and punishments in which ye human race was to be entangled; — This grace itself was given us in Christ before ye ages belonging toward ye world (2 Timothy 1:9). — And so ye Papists sense must be rejected, who here interpret grace as an infused quality or habit — whether ye habit belonging toward charity or another distinct out from charity. — First, therefore, when ye divine writings say we have been saved by grace, by grace stands as to be understood nothing but Gods mercy and free favor toward us. — Titus 3:4). — 2:4; — We mean rather ye acts belonging toward divine benevolence and philanthropy by which God pitied ye fallen human race when He saw it wholly sunk in eternal ruin and unable to be freed out from it unless He Himself came to its aid (Ephesians 1:5; — toward that would stand even if ye human had never been received into grace. — By this we do not mean that general beneficence belonging toward God by which all created things stand as conserved and governed; — Since our salvation and Gods friendship stand as wholly desperate whether we turn to ourselves or to all or any other creatures — because Gods justice, whose precept we violated, cannot otherwise be satisfied — ye first principle belonging toward this friendship and belonging toward our salvation stands as truly Gods grace. — The principles belonging toward human salvation stand as ye grace belonging toward paternal mercy, belonging toward fraternal redemption, and belonging toward Gods heavenly calling. — II.

title: III–V. Paternal mercy as first principle; object is the whole human race as miserable and stained by sin
latin: III. Gratia paternae MISERATIONIS est primum humanae salutis principium, quo Deus totum genus humanum ita complectitur, ut velit omnes homines salvos fieri, eisque secundum sapientiam & iustitiam suam media salutis amplissima ordinet ac determinet. Huius primi salutis nostrae principii propria sedes est Gen. 3:8,15; Ioh. 3:16; 1 Tim. 2:4; Tit. 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9. IV. Est autem hic considerandum eius obiectum & modus. V. Obiectum gratiae miserationis est totum genus humanum, ut miserum & peccato inquinatum. Hoc enim Servator noster Ioh. 3:16 docet vocabulo mundi. Nam certum est, hic voce mundi intelligi non totum systema caeli & terrae cum omnibus incolis, divinitus e nihilo productum, sed genus humanum duntaxat. Iam vero in sacris literis haec vox aliquando significat genus humanum universe, aliquando certam illius partem, & quidem vel credentes duntaxat, qui e toto mundo ad regnum Dei colliguntur, vel impios duntaxat, qui e toto mundo condemnantur. Manifestum etiam est, vocem mundi hic non intelligi hoc ultimo significatu, quo accipitur Ioh. 17:9 & Ioh. 14:17. Nec tamen Christus hic per mundum intelligit electos tantum, prout iam a mundo separati sunt: sed totum genus humanum universe sumtum, prout natura in peccato iacet, & prout communiter per euangelium ad poenitentiam & fidem in Christum vocatur, secundum illud Marci 16:15 & 1 Ioh. 2:2. Quanquam vero Deus totum mundum universe ita dilexerit: tamen haec dilectio peculiariter ac praecipue respicit credentes. Distinguimus tres status hominis post lapsum: primus naturae seu communis corruptionis; alter gratiae seu regenerationis; tertius impoenitentiae sive finalis indurationis, ubi tandem dilectio Dei sistit & mera ira & iudicium in contumaces redundat.
english: III. The grace of paternal MERCY is the first principle of human salvation, by which God so embraces the whole human race that He wills all humans to be saved, and according to His wisdom and justice orders and determines for them the amplest means of salvation. The proper seats of this first principle are Genesis 3:8,15; John 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:4; Titus 2:11; 2 Peter 3:9.

IV. Here its object and mode are to be considered. V. The object of the grace of mercy is the whole human race, as miserable and stained by sin. Our Savior teaches this by the word world in John 3:16. For it is certain that world here does not mean the whole system of heaven and earth with all its inhabitants produced from nothing by God, but only the human race. In the sacred writings this word sometimes signifies the human race universally, sometimes a certain part of it — either only believers gathered from the whole world into Gods kingdom, or only the impious condemned from the whole world.

It is also plain that world here is not taken in that last sense of John 17:9 and 14:17. Nor does Christ here mean by world only the elect as already separated from the world, but the whole human race taken universally, as by nature it lies in sin, and as it is commonly called through the gospel to repentance and faith in Christ (Mark 16:15; 1 John 2:2). Yet although God so loved the whole world universally, this love peculiarly and chiefly regards believers.

We distinguish three post-fall states of the human: first, of nature or common corruption; second, of grace or regeneration; third, of impenitence or final hardening, where at last Gods love stops and sheer wrath and judgment overflow upon the obstinate.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): third, belonging toward impenitence or final hardening, where at last Gods love stops and sheer wrath and judgment overflow upon ye obstinate. — second, belonging toward grace or regeneration; — first, belonging toward nature or common corruption; — We distinguish three post-fall states belonging toward ye human: — Yet although God so loved ye whole world universally, this love peculiarly and chiefly regards believers. — 1 John 2:2). — Nor does Christ here mean by world only ye elect as already separated out from ye world, but ye whole human race taken universally, as by nature it lies in sin, and as it stands as commonly called through ye gospel to repentance and faith in Christ (Mark 16:15; — It stands as also plain that same which world here stands as not taken in that same which last sense belonging toward John 17:9 and 14:17. — In ye sacred writings this word sometimes signifies ye human race universally, sometimes a certain part belonging toward it — either only believers gathered out from ye whole world into Gods kingdom, or only ye impious condemned out from ye whole world. — For it stands as certain that same which world here does not mean ye whole system belonging toward heaven and earth with all its inhabitants produced out from nothing by God, but only ye human race. — Our Savior teaches this by ye word world in John 3:16. — The object belonging toward ye grace belonging toward mercy stands as ye whole human race, as miserable and stained by sin. — V. — Here its object and mode stand as to be considered. — IV. — 2 Peter 3:9. — Titus 2:11; — 1 Timothy 2:4; — John 3:16; — The proper seats belonging toward this first principle stand as Genesis 3:8,15; — The grace belonging toward paternal MERCY stands as ye first principle belonging toward human salvation, by which God so embraces ye whole human race that same which He wills all humans to be saved, and according to His wisdom and justice orders and determines toward them ye amplest means belonging toward salvation. — III. — Latin anchors: Gratia, paternae, MISERATIONIS, primum, humanae, salutis, principium, totum, genus, humanum, complectitur, velit, omnes, homines, salvos, fieri, eisque, secundum, sapientiam, iustitiam — Objectum stands as totum genus humanum ut miserum & peccato inquinatum; mundus stands as human race not cosmos; electos not only; tres status post lapsum: naturae, gratiae, indurationis.

title: VI. From the object: love of all and of some; no clash with election
latin: VI. Ex iis vero, quae de obiecto gratiae miserationis divinae diximus, duo potissimum manifesta fiunt. Primum est, de quo alioquin ingens controversia agitatur, utrum videlicet Deus omnes, an vero aliquos duntaxat homines ita dilexerit? Quis enim negaverit Deum credentes, quos etiam ab aeterno elegit & agnovit, singulariter ac prae caeteris omnibus hominibus dilexisse? Quis vero etiam affirmarit, Deum infideles, etiamsi in sua incredulitate sine poenitentia permanerent, quando iam eos iudicavit & condemnavit, tamen ita diligere? Quis vero etiam ex adverso assereret, Deum eos nullo prorsus modo dilexisse, quibus dilectionem & gratiam suam tam saepe & varie, tam serio & ex animo offert, quibus etiam eam ipsam ob causam tam vehementer irascitur, eosque iudicat & condemnat, quod in Filium non credunt & dilectionem ac gratiam aspernantur & reiiciunt? Alterum vero est, quod haec dilectio Dei, qua totum mundum complectitur, non pugnet cum electione filiorum Dei, minimeque sequatur, si Deus totum mundum ita dilexerit, etiam totum propterea elegisse ad salutem. Hic enim locum habent illa Servatoris dicta Ioh. 15:19; 13:18; Matth. 22:14. Nam electio distinguit primum filios Dei, quos per gratiam suam salute donat, a reliquo mundo, qui sua propria culpa in incredulitate sua manet.
english: VI. From what we have said about the object of the divine grace of mercy, two things especially become plain.

First is the great controversy whether God so loved all humans, or only some. Who will deny that God singularly loved believers, whom He also elected and acknowledged from eternity, above all other humans? Who will affirm that God so loves unbelievers who remain without repentance in their unbelief, once He has already judged and condemned them? Who on the other side will assert that God in no way loved those to whom He so often, variously, seriously, and from the heart offers His love and grace — and against whom He is so vehemently angry, judging and condemning them precisely because they do not believe in the Son and spurn and reject love and grace?

Second: this love of God that embraces the whole world does not clash with the election of Gods children, and it by no means follows that if God so loved the whole world He therefore also elected the whole to salvation. Here the Saviors sayings in John 15:19; 13:18; Matthew 22:14 have place. For election first distinguishes the children of God, whom He gifts with salvation by His grace, from the remaining world that by its own fault remains in unbelief.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): For election first distinguishes ye children belonging toward God, whom He gifts with salvation by His grace, out from ye remaining world that by its own fault remains in unbelief. — Matthew 22:14 have place. — 13:18; — Here ye Saviors sayings in John 15:19; — this love belonging toward God that embraces ye whole world does not clash with ye election belonging toward Gods children, and it by no means follows that if God so loved ye whole world He therefore also elected ye whole to salvation. — Who will deny that God singularly loved believers, whom He also elected and acknowledged out from eternity, above all other humans? Who will affirm that God so loves unbelievers who remain without repentance in their unbelief, once He has already judged and condemned them? Who on ye other side will assert that God in no way loved those to whom He so often, variously, seriously, and out from ye heart offers His love and grace — and against whom He stands as so vehemently angry, judging and condemning them precisely because they do not believe in ye Son and spurn and reject love and grace? Second: — First stands as ye great controversy whether God so loved all humans, or only some. — From what we have said about ye object belonging toward ye divine grace belonging toward mercy, two things especially become plain. — VI.

title: VII–IX. Mode of mercy: amplitude in gift, demand, and promise
latin: VII. Modus gratiae miserationis consistit in illius amplitudine ac determinatione. VIII. Amplitudo eius posita est in dono, in postulato & in promisso. IX. Primum dono superabundans Dei erga nos dilectio manifesta fit. Nam non dilexit nos propter meritum aliquod nostrum, quod ipsi priores aliquid dederimus quod nobis retribueret, Rom. 11:35, aut quod eum dilexerimus priores, 1 Ioh. 4:19, sed multo magis quod cum meram iram & indignationem commeriti eramus, & quod in principio ab ipso acceperamus, nempe imaginem ipsius, quantum in nobis erat, perdideramus; imo & illud quod ipsi debebamus, nempe timorem, honorem, dilectionem, obedientiam, imo & animam corpusque nostrum interverteramus: cum e servis inimici facti eramus, cumque nobis mercedem peccatorum, mortem & infernum, dare potuisset: nobis imaginem substantiae suae, Filium suum unigenitum dedit. Singulis gratia fuit Israeli dari servum Mosen & Davidem: quanto maior gratia est nobis dari non servum, sed Filium Dei, eumque unigenitum? Et quidem non ut tantum sit propheta & doctor salutis, ut fingunt Socinistae, aut servator terrenus, ut Iudaei: sed ut sit aeternus Servator, Pontifex & Rex, qui se ipsum, tanquam verum sacrificium propitiatorium, in mortem obtulit pro nobis, non ut nos ex Aegypto in Chananaeam, sed e morte & inferno in caelum traduceret. Secundo patet gratia divinae miserationis ex eo quod a nobis postulat. Nam Deus non exigit a nobis sacrificia & dona Levitica, non servilem & coactam obedientiam legis Mosaicae, sed filialem obedientiam fidei. Atque hoc ita a nobis postulat, ut illud simul per Spiritum suum in nobis velit operari. Tertio vero omnium maxime elucet e promisso nobis in Filio Dei facto: ut omnes qui in ipsum credunt non pereant, sed vitam aeternam habeant.
english: VII. The mode of the grace of mercy consists in its amplitude and determination. VIII. Its amplitude is set in the gift, in what is demanded, and in the promise.

IX. First, Gods overflowing love toward us is made plain by the gift. For He did not love us because of any merit of ours, as if we had first given Him something He should repay (Romans 11:35), or because we loved Him first (1 John 4:19), but much more because when we had deserved sheer wrath and indignation, and had as far as in us lay destroyed the image we had received from Him at the beginning — yes, and overturned what we owed Him, fear, honor, love, obedience, even our soul and body — when from servants we had become enemies, and when He could have given us the wages of sins, death and hell: He gave us the image of His substance, His only-begotten Son. It was grace to Israel to be given the servant Moses and David: how much greater the grace that we are given not a servant but the Son of God, and Him only-begotten — and not merely as prophet and teacher of salvation, as the Socinians invent, or as an earthly savior, as the Jews, but as eternal Savior, High Priest, and King, who offered Himself as a true propitiatory sacrifice unto death for us, not to lead us from Egypt into Canaan but from death and hell into heaven.

Second, the grace of divine mercy is plain from what He demands of us. For God does not exact Levitical sacrifices and gifts, nor servile and forced obedience to the Mosaic law, but the filial obedience of faith — and He demands this in such a way that He also wills to work it in us by His Spirit.
Third, and most of all, it shines from the promise made to us in the Son of God: that all who believe in Him should not perish but have eternal life.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): For God does not exact Levitical sacrifices and gifts, nor servile and forced obedience to ye Mosaic law, but ye filial obedience belonging toward faith — and He demands this in such a way that He also wills to work it in us by His Spirit. — Second, ye grace belonging toward divine mercy stands as plain out from what He demands belonging toward us. — how much greater ye grace that we stand as given not a servant but ye Son belonging toward God, and Him only-begotten — and not merely as prophet and teacher belonging toward salvation, as ye Socinians invent, or as an earthly savior, as ye Jews, but as eternal Savior, High Priest, and King, who offered Himself as a true propitiatory sacrifice unto death toward us, not to lead us out from Egypt into Canaan but out from death and hell into heaven. — It was grace to Israel to be given ye servant Moses and David: — He gave us ye image belonging toward His substance, His only-begotten Son. — For He did not love us because belonging toward any merit belonging toward ours, as if we had first given Him something He should repay (Romans 11:35), or because we loved Him first (1 John 4:19), but much more because when we had deserved sheer wrath and indignation, and had as far as in us lay destroyed ye image we had received out from Him at ye beginning — yes, and overturned what we owed Him, fear, honor, love, obedience, even our soul and body — when out from servants we had become enemies, and when He could have given us ye wages belonging toward sins, death and hell: — First, Gods overflowing love toward us stands as made plain by ye gift. — IX. — Its amplitude stands as set in ye gift, in what stands as demanded, and in ye promise. — VIII. — The mode belonging toward ye grace belonging toward mercy consists in its amplitude and determination. — VII.

title: Determination of mercy: only in the Son; by repentance and faith; by the light of Word and Spirit
latin: Determinatio gratiae miserationis est, qua Deus eam per sapientiam & iustitiam suam ita limitat, emetitur & ordinat, ut hominem peccatorem non sine Christo Filio suo aut extra eum, neque sine poenitentia & fide, sed hanc secundum iustitiam suam postulando & vitam in Christo promittendo, per gratiam vero utramque largiendo, in amicitiam suam recipiat, a peccato absolvat & vita aeterna donet. Tria igitur sunt, quibus divina sapientia & iustitia philanthropiam universalem restringit ac limitat. 1. Deus quidem dilexit mundum peccato inquinatum, non tamen ita ut sine Filio aut extra Filium diligat, aut sine satisfactione & expiatione peccata ei remittat & eum beet, sed tantum in Filio & per Filium, quem dedit in mediatorem & propitiatorem. 2. Posteaquam Deus Filium suum dedit in reconciliationem, mundum ita in eo dilexit atque hoc pacto per eum sibi reconciliavit, ut non sine poenitentia & fide peccatorum remissionem consequeretur. 3. Deus mundum vi novi illius foederis gratiae in Christo ita dilexit, ut non solum secundum iustitiam suam obedientiam exegerit & vitam promiserit, sicut in veteri foedere legis: verum etiam per gratiam suam, tum illud quod in Euangelio postulat, nempe obedientiam fidei, tum quod in eo promittit, nempe certissimam consolationem remissionis omnium peccatorum & vitae aeternae, efficaciter operari & largiri velit — ita tamen, ut fidem non per nudam omnipotentiam suam & mera miracula in hominibus operetur, aut eos quasi violenter ad fidem cogat, sed per lumen verbi & Spiritus eius in Euangelio.
english: The determination of the grace of mercy is that by which God, through His wisdom and justice, so limits, measures, and orders it that He receives the sinful human into His friendship, absolves from sin, and gifts with eternal life — not without Christ His Son or outside Him, nor without repentance and faith, but by demanding this according to His justice and promising life in Christ, and by grace bestowing both.

Three things therefore restrain and limit the universal philanthropy by divine wisdom and justice. First: God loved the world stained by sin, yet not so as to love it without the Son or outside the Son, or to remit sins and bless it without satisfaction and expiation, but only in the Son and through the Son, whom He gave as mediator and propitiator.
Second: after God gave His Son for reconciliation, He so loved the world in Him and reconciled it to Himself through Him that remission of sins is not obtained without repentance and faith.

Third: by the force of that new covenant of grace in Christ God so loved the world that He not only, according to His justice, exacted obedience and promised life as in the old covenant of the law, but also by His grace wills to work and bestow both what the gospel demands — the obedience of faith — and what it promises — the most certain consolation of remission of all sins and of eternal life; yet not by bare omnipotence and mere miracles, or by forcing humans as it were violently to faith, but by the light of Word and Spirit in the gospel.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): yet not by bare omnipotence and mere miracles, or by forcing humans as it were violently to faith, but by ye light belonging toward Word and Spirit in ye gospel. — by ye force belonging toward that new covenant belonging toward grace in Christ God so loved ye world that He not only, according to His justice, exacted obedience and promised life as in ye old covenant belonging toward ye law, but also by His grace wills to work and bestow both what ye gospel demands — ye obedience belonging toward faith — and what it promises — ye most certain consolation belonging toward remission belonging toward all sins and belonging toward eternal life; — Third: — after God gave His Son toward reconciliation, He so loved ye world in Him and reconciled it to Himself through Him that remission belonging toward sins stands as not obtained without repentance and faith. — Second: — God loved ye world stained by sin, yet not so as to love it without ye Son or outside ye Son, or to remit sins and bless it without satisfaction and expiation, but only in ye Son and through ye Son, whom He gave as mediator and propitiator. — First: — Three things therefore restrain and limit ye universal philanthropy by divine wisdom and justice. — The determination belonging toward ye grace belonging toward mercy stands as that by which God, through His wisdom and justice, so limits, measures, and orders it that He receives ye sinful human into His friendship, absolves out from sin, and gifts with eternal life — not without Christ His Son or outside Him, nor without repentance and faith, but by demanding this according to His justice and promising life in Christ, and by grace bestowing both.

title: Corollaries: unequal light of grace; election mystery; decree ordered to Christs merit and means
latin: Atque ex dictis sequentia fluunt confectaria. 1. Universali gratiae & philanthropiae, qua Deus mundum dilexit, & merito Christi non repugnat, quod Deus uni populo aut regioni maiorem lucem, adeoque & maiorem gratiam ac dilectionem concedit quam aliis, adeoque plus minusve secundum diversitatem aetatum & temporum. 2. Neque repugnat dilectioni Dei & merito Christi, quod vel eodem tempore & loco uni homini maiorem lucem & gratiam quam alii concedit, & quidem unicuique secundum mensuram donorum Christi. 3. In hac dispositione Dei, quando, ubi & quomodo lucem & efficaciam verbi & Spiritus sui in mundo lucere & operari sinit, consistit proprie summum mysterium electionis filiorum Dei. Nam hac secundum consilium & propositum suum Deus hominibus lapsis in Christo ab aeterno misericorditer dispensare constituit hanc gratuitam lucem verbi & Spiritus sui. 4. Etiamsi Deus neque praevisione operum, neque fidei, ulliusve alterius conditionis animalis in hominibus peccatoribus, sed sola immerita misericordia sua motus sit, ut quosdam ex iis ad vitam eligeret: tamen hoc decretum electionis non simpliciter absolutum dici haud potest; quia, etiamsi ex parte hominis animalis nulla illius determinatio aut conditio est, tamen est aliqua ex parte Dei, qui illud ad meritum Christi & media — praedicationem Euangelii puta & fidem hoc applicantia — ipse met adstrinxit.
english: From what has been said the following corollaries flow.

1. It does not clash with the universal grace and philanthropy by which God loved the world, nor with Christs merit, that God grants one people or region greater light — and so also greater grace and love — than others, and more or less according to the diversity of ages and times.
2. Nor does it clash with Gods love and Christs merit that even at the same time and place He grants one human greater light and grace than another, each according to the measure of Christs gifts.

3. In this disposition of God — when, where, and how He lets the light and efficacy of His Word and Spirit shine and work in the world — consists properly the highest mystery of the election of Gods children. For according to His counsel and purpose God from eternity mercifully appointed to dispense to fallen humans in Christ this free light of Word and Spirit.

4. Even though God was moved not by foresight of works or of faith or of any other animal condition in sinful humans, but by His alone unmerited mercy, to elect some of them to life: still this decree of election cannot simply be called absolute; for although on the animals side in the human there is no determination or condition of it, yet there is some on Gods side, who Himself bound it to Christs merit and to the means — namely the preaching of the gospel and the faith that applies it.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): toward although on ye animals side in ye human there stands as no determination or condition belonging toward it, yet there stands as some on Gods side, who Himself bound it to Christs merit and to ye means — namely ye preaching belonging toward ye gospel and ye faith that applies it. — still this decree belonging toward election cannot simply be called absolute; — Even though God was moved not by foresight belonging toward works or belonging toward faith or belonging toward any other animal condition in sinful humans, but by His alone unmerited mercy, to elect some belonging toward them to life: — 4. — For according to His counsel and purpose God out from eternity mercifully appointed to dispense to fallen humans in Christ this free light belonging toward Word and Spirit. — In this disposition belonging toward God — when, where, and how He lets ye light and efficacy belonging toward His Word and Spirit shine and work in ye world — consists properly ye highest mystery belonging toward ye election belonging toward Gods children. — 3. — Nor does it clash with Gods love and Christs merit that even at ye same time and place He grants one human greater light and grace than another, each according to ye measure belonging toward Christs gifts. — 2. — It does not clash with ye universal grace and philanthropy by which God loved ye world, nor with Christs merit, that God grants one people or region greater light — and so also greater grace and love — than others, and more or less according to ye diversity belonging toward ages and times. — 1. — From what has been said ye following corollaries flow.

title: Cause of damnation in humans themselves; Cap.1 close toward Cap.2 on the grace of redemption
latin: Reprobatio vero est iusta sententia iudicii Dei in omnes impoenitentes infideles. Primo, culpa non est Patris. Nam Filium suum in hunc mundum misit, non ut eum iudicet, sed ut servet. Iure quidem, secundum rigorem iustitiae suae, Filium suum mittere potuisset ad iudicandum & condemnandum mundum ob peccata in legem, quia totus in malo iacet: at ex mera gratia ipsum primo misit non ad iudicium. Causa proxima & princeps damnationis est in ipsis hominibus. Dominus non loquitur simpliciter de incredulitate habituali & innata, sed de actuali, affectata, contumaci cum impoenitentia perpetua coniuncta. Haec vero est caput omnium peccatorum, quod Deus per iustitiam & veritatem suam non potest non damnare. Ratio est, quia non credunt in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei: extra quod nomen nulla salus. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum est, amorem tenebrarum & odium lucis — causam propriam iudicii & damnationis hominum — non nisi in ipsis quaerendam esse. Vide eximium Theologum D. Iohannem Bergium in explicatione dicti Sic Deus dilexit mundum, de causis salutis & damnationis humanae Berolini 1629 edita. CAPUT SECUNDUM sequitur de gratia redemtionis.
english: Reprobation is the just sentence of Gods judgment upon all impenitent unbelievers. First, the fault is not the Fathers. For He sent His Son into this world not to judge it but to save it. By right, according to the rigor of His justice, He could have sent His Son to judge and condemn the world for sins against the law, because the whole lies in evil: yet from sheer grace He first sent Him not for judgment.

The proximate and chief cause of damnation is in humans themselves. The Lord does not speak simply of habitual and innate unbelief, but of actual, affected, obstinate unbelief joined with perpetual impenitence. This is the head of all sins, which God by His justice and truth cannot but condemn. The reason is that they do not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God: outside which name there is no salvation.

From all this it is plain that love of darkness and hatred of light — the proper cause of humans judgment and damnation — is to be sought only in themselves. See the excellent theologian Dr. Johann Bergius in his explanation of the saying So God loved the world, on the causes of human salvation and damnation, published at Berlin in 1629.
CHAPTER TWO follows, on the grace of redemption.
